newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Beijing undecided on Hong Kong's future leader - paper.
newsitem.headline: Beijing undecided on Hong Kong's future leader - paper.

text.p: China has not made up its mind who it would like to lead Hong Kong after Beijing regains sovereignty over the territory next year, a Hong Kong newspaper said on Tuesday, citing internal Chinese documents.

Less than two months before the chief executive is expected to be selected, shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa is considered the frontrunner for the job but Beijing still has doubts about his suitability, the Hong Kong Standard said.

Internal central government profiles on the magnate noted his international renown, his ties with Britain's governing Conservative Party and his links with influential bodies in the United States and Japan, the paper quoted Chinese sources as saying.
Tung also had close personal ties with late Taiwan President Chiang Ching-kuo, it said.
Tung, yet to announce whether he will run for the job, is one of several unofficial candidates named so far.
Many analysts believe Beijing signalled it favoured him in January when President Jiang Zemin singled out Tung in a room full of Hong Kong advisers and pointedly shook his hand.

The new chief executive, who will take over from Governor Chris Patten on July 1, 1997, will be chosen by a 400-member Selection Committee, itself to be named by Beijing's Preparatory Committee overseeing the handover.
Britain returns Hong Kong to China at midnight next June 30, ending a century and half of colonial rule.
Last week, Hong Kong's Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang resigned after announcing he would run for the chief executive's job.
In addition to Yang, prominent lawyer Lo Tak-shing has also declared his candidacy.
Hong Kong's favourite is Patten's deputy, Anson Chan, but her close association with the British administration is widely regarded as ruling her out in Beijing's eyes.
